chapters.title: A question rides a rocket
chapters.story: Imagine a small robot tucked inside a spacecraft at Cape Canaveral. Its name is Opportunity, and it has a question: did water once change the rocks on Mars? On 8 July 2003, a Delta II rocket lifts it away from Earth. The rocket will not travel all the way with it. Opportunity's spacecraft will cross space for more than six months. This opening scene is a simple diagram. Open the mission atlas to follow the archived SPICE spacecraft path through space.
chapters.fact: The launch time is recorded to the second. The separate mission atlas plots archived SPICE spacecraft positions; this opening scene is schematic.

chapters.title: A hole in one on Mars

ground.title: Inside Eagle Crater
ground.note: Opportunity's first 360° colour panorama, published by NASA on 2 February 2004. A rover-camera view, not a surveyed position on the orbital map.

image.alt: Opportunity looks back at its empty landing platform and tracks on Mars

chapters.story: Now we are above Mars. Opportunity falls through the thin atmosphere, protected by a heat shield, parachute, and airbags. It bounces across Meridiani Planum and comes to rest inside a small crater: Eagle. When the airbags retract, its landing platform opens like a flower. Opportunity drives away, but the platform stays here. Switch to the rover's view to look around the crater; this panorama was taken days after landing.
chapters.fact: NASA gives the landing site as 1.9483° S, 354.47417° E. The Eagle Crater platform is visible in later orbital imagery.

chapters.title: What did the rocks remember?

ground.title: Looking back into Eagle Crater
ground.note: Opportunity's 360° 'Lion King' panorama, captured on sols 58 and 60 and released 14 April 2004. The empty lander is visible inside the crater.

image.alt: Opportunity's close view of the Berry Bowl rock and its round hematite grains

chapters.story: Let's stay with Eagle Crater for a moment. Opportunity looks closely at layered rock and tiny round grains that the team nicknames blueberries. The grains contain a mineral called hematite. Together with the rock layers and their chemistry, they help scientists tell an old story: water once shaped this ground. The rover has found evidence of water, not evidence of living things. Inspect the close-up, then look back into the crater in a panorama taken after the rover drove out.
chapters.fact: The rover found evidence of ancient water. This does not mean it found life.

chapters.title: A new crater on the horizon

ground.title: At Spirit Point
ground.note: Opportunity's Pancam mosaic after arriving at Endeavour's rim in August 2011. This is a directional view, not a 360° panorama.

image.alt: Opportunity's panorama on arrival at Endeavour Crater's rim

chapters.story: Opportunity was designed for 90 Martian days, yet it keeps travelling for years. On 9 August 2011, it reaches the western rim of enormous Endeavour Crater at a place called Spirit Point. In the rover's photograph, you can look across the rim. On our globe, the marker is at Endeavour's official centre, because the arrival photograph does not give us a precise rover coordinate here. The map and the camera tell different, complementary parts of the story.
chapters.fact: The marker on the globe shows Endeavour's official centre, not Opportunity's arrival point on its rim.

chapters.title: The last message home

ground.title: Perseverance Valley
ground.note: Opportunity's final 360° Pancam panorama, acquired 13 May–10 June 2018. Some frames remain black and white because imaging was unfinished.

image.alt: NASA's final traverse map of Opportunity from Eagle Crater to Perseverance Valley

chapters.story: Our map follows Opportunity to Perseverance Valley, on Endeavour's western rim. Here the rover photographs a full circle around itself. Then, in June 2018, a dust storm spreads across Mars. Sunlight fades, and Opportunity's solar panels cannot make enough power. Its last signal reaches Earth on 10 June. Look around its final panorama. The empty parts of some frames are real: the rover never finished sending every colour image.
chapters.fact: Last contact is not the same as the date NASA declared the mission complete. The rover travelled 45.16 km in total.

chapters.title: A machine can leave a question answered

ground.title: Perseverance Valley
ground.note: Opportunity's final 360° Pancam panorama, acquired 13 May–10 June 2018. The rover's exact resting point is not claimed here.

image.alt: NASA's final traverse map of Opportunity from Eagle Crater to Perseverance Valley

chapters.story: For months, people on Earth keep listening for Opportunity. No new signal comes. On 13 February 2019, NASA ends the mission. The rover remains in Perseverance Valley. Far away, its landing platform remains in Eagle Crater, and other entry hardware lies where it fell. These machines were left on Mars, but their discoveries came home: this world once had places shaped by water. Which object would you choose to tell the next story?
chapters.fact: Opportunity's status is inactive. The final area is backed by NASA imagery, but this edition does not invent a pinpoint coordinate for the rover.
